summary: This standards-track RFC defines how the Opus interactive speech and audio codec is encapsulated in Ogg, so Opus-encoded data can be stored in an Ogg logical bitstream.

plainLanguage.summary: Ogg Opus describes how audio compressed with the Opus codec is written into an Ogg file or stream. It defines two headers at the start, a way of counting samples so a player knows where it is in time, and a set of channel layouts.

questions: how is opus stored in ogg files
what is the opus file extension
what is the opus channel mapping family
subtitle: How Opus audio is packed into Ogg files and streams: headers, timing, channel layouts and metadata.

tldr.problem: Opus produces compressed audio packets, but a player needs a container that carries them with timing, metadata and a way to seek.
tldr.mechanism: The encapsulation puts two mandatory header packets, an identification header and a comment header, at the start of the logical stream, then packs the audio data packets into Ogg pages, with the granule position of each page giving the sample count.
tldr.outcome: Opus audio can be stored and streamed in the same form, with fast seeking, metadata and the ability to be multiplexed with other codecs. RFC 7845 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 8486.

today: RFC 7845 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2016. It updates RFC 5334 to add the Opus codec identifier, and it was later updated by RFC 8486, which added ambisonics to the Ogg Opus container. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the Encapsulation Adds
sections.content:
Opus is a low-latency audio codec optimised for both voice and general-purpose audio, specified in RFC 6716. This document defines how Opus data is carried in a continuous logical Ogg bitstream, as defined in RFC 3533.

Ogg encapsulation gives Opus a long-term storage format with the features a codec needs in practice: metadata, fast and accurate seeking, corruption detection, the ability to recover after an error, low overhead, and the ability to multiplex Opus with other codecs, including video, with little buffering. It is also a live streaming format that can be delivered over a reliable stream-oriented transport without needing all the data, or even the total length of the data, up front, and in a form identical to the on-disk storage format.

An Ogg bitstream is a series of pages, each holding data from one or more packets. Pages are the unit of multiplexing. Each page belongs to one logical stream and carries a capture pattern and checksum, flags marking the start and end of the logical stream, and a granule position giving an absolute position in the stream to aid seeking. A single page can hold up to 65,025 octets of packet data from up to 255 different packets. Packets can be split across pages, so a packet may be larger than a page. Each page carries lacing values that show how the data is split into packets, so a demultiplexer can recover the packet boundaries without looking at the encoded data.

This encapsulation defines what goes inside the packets, which headers are needed, how the packets are organised into a logical stream, and how the granule position is to be interpreted. It does not restate the Ogg container format itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Opus compresses audio into packets. Ogg is the container that holds those packets and adds what a player needs: a place for metadata, a way to know the time, and a way to find any point in the file quickly.

sections.title: Packet Organization
sections.content:
An Ogg Opus stream starts with two mandatory header packets. The first packet in the logical bitstream MUST contain the identification header, which identifies the stream as Opus audio. It is placed alone on the first page of the logical bitstream, completes on that page, and that page has its beginning-of-stream flag set.

The second packet MUST contain the comment header, which holds user-supplied metadata. It MAY span several pages, starting on the second page of the logical stream, but it MUST finish the page on which it completes.

Every page after that is an audio data page. Each audio data packet holds one Opus packet for each of N different streams, where N is typically one for mono or stereo and MAY be larger for multichannel audio. The value of N is given in the identification header and is fixed for the whole logical bitstream. The first N - 1 Opus packets are packed one after another using the self-delimiting framing from Appendix B of RFC 6716, and the remaining Opus packet is packed at the end using the regular undelimited framing from Section 3 of that RFC. All the Opus packets in one Ogg packet MUST have the same duration, and an implementation SHOULD treat a packet with a different duration as malformed.

The table of contents sequence at the start of each Opus packet gives the coding mode, audio bandwidth, channel count, duration and number of frames per packet. The coding mode is one of SILK, Hybrid or Constrained Energy Lapsed Transform, and the combination of coding mode, bandwidth and frame size is called the configuration of the packet.

Packets are placed into pages in order until the end of the stream, and an audio data packet may span a page boundary. A live stream joined part way through may have its headers pasted on the front, in which case the first audio data page carries the continued-packet flag. If that flag is set and either the previous page does not end in a continued packet or the page sequence numbers are not consecutive, a demuxer MUST NOT attempt to decode the first packet on the page. A zero-octet audio data packet MUST be treated as a malformed Opus packet.

A logical stream ends with a page marked end of stream, but a demuxer must be ready for truncated streams with no such page. If a packet continues onto a following page and either the next page does not have the continued-packet flag, or there is no next page, or the page sequence numbers are not consecutive, the demuxer MUST NOT attempt to decode that packet. No page may follow a page marked end of stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The stream begins with an identification header on its own page and a comment header after it. Everything else is audio. Each audio packet holds one Opus packet per channel group, and the packets are packed into Ogg pages, which may split them anywhere. A reader that finds a broken or missing page must not guess at the missing audio.

sections.title: Granule Position, Pre-skip and Timing
sections.content:
The granule position MUST be zero for the identification header page and for the page where the comment header completes. The granule position of an audio data page gives the total number of PCM samples in the stream up to and including the last fully decodable sample of the last packet completed on that page. A page entirely spanned by one packet that completes on a later page has no granule position, and the field is set to the special value -1 in two's complement.

Granule positions count PCM samples at a fixed rate of 48 kHz per channel, so a stereo stream does not count twice as fast as a mono one. A decoder can run at another sample rate, but every Opus packet encodes samples at a rate that evenly divides 48 kHz, so the value always counts samples as if the decoding rate were 48 kHz. A packet's duration is any multiple of 2.5 ms up to 120 ms, encoded in the table of contents sequence, and the number of samples a decoder returns matches that duration exactly. A demuxer can therefore work backwards or forwards from a page with a known granule position and assign a position to every packet, or even every sample.

Pre-skip. Decoding introduces latency, for overlap in the CELT mode, stereo mixing in the SILK mode, and resampling, and the encoder may add more. The first samples the decoder produces are padding rather than real audio. They still have to be decoded, because Opus is a predictive codec and each frame depends on the recent history of decoder inputs, but a player should skip them. The pre-skip field in the identification header gives the number of samples that SHOULD be skipped at the start. It need not be a multiple of 2.5 ms, may be smaller than one packet, and may span several packets. The same field can be used to crop an already encoded stream, where a value of at least 3840 samples, 80 ms, gives the decoder enough history to converge.

The PCM sample position is the granule position minus the pre-skip. For example, if the granule position of the first audio data page is 59,971 and the pre-skip is 11,971, the PCM sample position of the last decoded sample from that page is 48,000. Dividing that by 48000.0 gives the playback time in seconds.

The page with the end-of-stream flag set may have a granule position that indicates the page holds less audio than decoding the final packet would give, which ends the stream somewhere other than a frame boundary. The number of samples discarded SHOULD be no larger than the number decoded from the last packet.

The granule position of the first audio data page with a completed packet MAY be larger than the number of samples in the packets completing on it, which allows a stream to be cropped or a live stream joined without rewriting the granule positions of all the later pages. It MUST NOT be smaller, unless that page has the end-of-stream flag set, because a demuxer could not work backwards and granule positions cannot be negative. An implementation MUST treat a stream as invalid if the granule position is smaller than the number of samples in the packets completing on the first such page.

Seeking is done with a bisection search for a page whose granule position matches the target, which with appropriate weighting takes one or two bisections on average even in a multi-gigabyte file. When seeking, an implementation SHOULD start decoding at least 3840 samples, 80 ms, before the target and discard the output, so that the audio is correct when the target is reached. This pre-roll is separate from the pre-skip at the start of the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Each page says how many samples have been played by the end of it, counted at 48 kHz. The header also says how many samples at the start are decoder padding rather than real sound, so a player skips them. Together these two numbers let a player work out the exact time of any point in the file.

sections.title: The Identification Header
sections.content:
The identification header begins with an 8-octet magic signature, the ASCII string "OpusHead", which identifies the codec. It starts with "Op" so that it cannot be confused with audio data, since that would be an invalid table of contents sequence.

The version number is 8 bits and MUST always be 1 for this specification. The upper four bits act as a major version and the lower four bits as a minor version, so a change in the minor version signals a compatible change. An implementation SHOULD accept any stream with a version number of 15 or less, and SHOULD assume a version number of 16 or greater is incompatible. The version 1 was chosen so that implementations would not treat the octet as a null terminator for the string.

The output channel count is 8 bits and gives the number of output channels, which may differ from the number of encoded channels and can change from packet to packet. It MUST NOT be zero, and the maximum depends on the channel mapping family, reaching 255.

The pre-skip is 16 bits, little endian, and gives the number of samples at 48 kHz to discard from the decoder output at the start of playback, and the number to subtract from a page's granule position to get its PCM sample position. When cropping the start of an existing stream, a pre-skip of at least 3840 samples, 80 ms, is RECOMMENDED so that the decoder converges completely.

The input sample rate is 32 bits, little endian, and is the sample rate of the original input before encoding. It is not the rate to use for playback. Opus can switch between internal bandwidths of 4, 6, 8, 12 and 20 kHz, and the reference decoder can decode any stream at 8, 12, 16, 24 or 48 kHz, and the original rate is not preserved by the lossy compression. A player SHOULD decode at 48 kHz if the hardware supports it, otherwise at the highest supported rate the hardware has, otherwise at the next higher supported rate and resample, and otherwise at 48 kHz and resample. The field is metadata for muxers, and a value of zero means unspecified. Implementations SHOULD support input sample rates between 8 kHz and 192 kHz inclusive, and may ignore rates outside that range by falling back to 48 kHz.

The output gain is 16 bits, signed, little endian, and is the gain to apply when decoding, stored as a Q7.8 fixed-point value in decibels. It is 20 times the base-10 logarithm of the factor by which to scale the decoder output. Players and media frameworks SHOULD apply it by default, and any other volume adjustment MUST be applied in addition to it. A muxer SHOULD set it to zero and apply any gain before encoding where possible. Its range is plus or minus 128 dB, which allows gain to be transferred between the header and the gain comment tags without saturating.

The channel mapping family is 8 bits and gives the order and meaning of the output channels. The channel mapping table follows, and is REQUIRED unless the family is 0. All the other fields are REQUIRED. An implementation SHOULD treat a stream as invalid if the identification header does not hold enough data for these fields, even when the magic signature is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The first header says what the file is, how many channels it has, how much of the start is decoder padding, what the original sample rate was, how loud to play it, and how the channels are arranged. It starts with the text OpusHead so that a program can recognise the format.

sections.title: Channel Mapping
sections.content:
An Ogg Opus stream maps a number of Opus streams, N, to a possibly larger number of decoded channels, M + N, and then to the output channels, C. The output channel count does not have to match the decoded channel count: one decoded channel may feed several output channels, and some decoded channels may feed none.

The channel mapping table holds the stream count N, the total number of streams encoded in each Ogg packet, which MUST NOT be zero because a demuxer could not otherwise recover the duration of a packet; for family 0 it defaults to 1 and is not coded. It holds the coupled stream count M, the number of streams whose decoders produce two channels, which MUST be no larger than N; for family 0 it defaults to C - 1 and is not coded. The total number of decoded channels, M + N, MUST be no larger than 255. Each Opus packet has an internal channel count of one or two that can change from packet to packet, since the encoder chooses it based on the bitrate and the audio, and any stream can be decoded as mono or stereo depending on how the decoder is initialised.

The channel mapping is one octet per output channel, saying which decoded channel feeds it. The value MUST be smaller than M + N or the special value 255. A value below 2M means the output comes from stream index divided by two, taking the left channel when the value is even and the right when it is odd. A value of 2M or more but below 255 means the output comes from stream index minus M, decoded as mono. A value of 255 means the output channel is pure silence.

Three mapping families are defined. Family 0 allows 1 or 2 channels and uses the RTP mapping: mono, or stereo with left and right. Its mapping table MUST be omitted. Family 1 allows 1 to 8 channels and uses the Vorbis channel order, assigning each channel to a speaker position in a conventional surround arrangement: mono; stereo; linear surround with left, centre and right; quadraphonic; 5.0; 5.1 with the low frequency effects channel; 6.1; and 7.1. This ordering differs from the WAVE and FLAC formats, so converting to or from them needs the output channels permuted. Family 255 allows 1 to 255 channels with no defined meaning; general-purpose players SHOULD NOT play such streams, though offline implementations may deinterleave them into one PCM file per channel. The remaining families, 2 to 254, are reserved, and a demuxer that meets one SHOULD behave as though it were 255.

A player MUST support any valid mapping with family 0 or 1, even when the channel count does not match the connected hardware, and SHOULD mix channels up or down as needed. The document gives downmix matrices for the multichannel families.
sections.plainLanguage: Opus stores audio in one or two channel streams, and the header says how those streams become the speakers you hear. Family 0 is mono or stereo, family 1 covers surround layouts up to 7.1, and family 255 means the channels have no agreed meaning.

sections.title: The Comment Header and Its Tags
sections.content:
The comment header starts with the 8-octet magic signature "OpusTags" and continues with data in the same format as the Vorbis comment header used in Ogg Vorbis, except that the final framing bit is not present. It holds a vendor string length, the vendor string as a UTF-8 string identifying the encoder and encapsulation implementation, a user comment list length, and then a length and a UTF-8 string for each user comment. The user comment strings use the NAME=value format with the recommended tag names such as ARTIST, TITLE, DATE and ALBUM.

Both length fields are REQUIRED. An implementation SHOULD treat a stream as invalid if the comment header does not hold enough data for them, or for the strings they describe. Making this check before allocating the memory to hold the data helps prevent a denial-of-service attack in which a small comment header claims to contain strings longer than the whole packet. Binary data that follows the comment list may be present; if the least significant bit of its first byte is 1, editors SHOULD preserve it, and if it is 0, the data may be treated as padding. The comment header can be arbitrarily large and may span many pages, so implementations MUST avoid allocating excessive memory; they MAY treat a stream as invalid if the comment header is larger than 125,829,120 octets, 120 MB, and MAY ignore individual comments that are not fully contained within the first 61,440 octets.

Two new comment tags are defined. R128_TRACK_GAIN gives the volume shift needed to normalise the track's volume during isolated playback and in random shuffle, and R128_ALBUM_GAIN gives the shift needed to normalise the volume when the track is played as part of a collection. Both are Q7.8 fixed-point numbers in decibels, as in the identification header's output gain field. The examples given are -573 and 111. A stream MUST NOT have more than one of each tag, and the values MUST be an integer from -32768 to 32767 inclusive, written in ASCII as a base 10 number with no whitespace, with a leading plus or minus sign allowed, leading zeros allowed, and no more than 6 characters in total.

If present, the two tags MUST correctly represent the R128 normalisation gain relative to the output gain field in the identification header, and a player that uses them MUST apply them in addition to the output gain. A tool that modifies the output gain field MUST also update or remove those tags. A muxer SHOULD put the gain it wants other tools to use by default into the output gain field rather than the comment tag. An Opus comment header SHOULD NOT contain the REPLAYGAIN tags, because the R128 normalisation is preferred, having a clear definition and wide adoption, and peak normalisation is hard to calculate reliably for a lossy codec.
sections.plainLanguage: The second header holds the metadata: who made the file, and tags such as the artist and title. It also holds two optional volume tags, for normalising one track or a whole album, which a player adds to the volume set in the first header.

sections.title: Packet Size Limits and Encoder Guidance
sections.content:
Technically valid Opus packets can be arbitrarily large because of the padding format, even though the amount of real data in them is bounded, and such a packet may be spread over a very large number of pages. When encoding, implementations SHOULD limit padding in audio data packets to no more than is needed to make a variable-bitrate stream constant bitrate. Demuxers SHOULD treat an audio data packet as invalid if it is larger than 61,440 octets per Opus stream, unless they have a specific reason to allow extra padding, and MUST avoid allocating excessive memory for a very large packet. A packet that is both larger than 61,440 octets and larger than 7,680 octets per Opus stream may be treated as invalid or partially processed. An extremely large packet could be a memory exhaustion attack or stream corruption.

The largest possible valid packet without padding is 61,298 times N minus 2 octets. With 255 streams that is 15,630,988 octets, spanning up to 61,298 pages, all but one of which would have a granule position of -1. The largest packet made entirely of useful data is 15,326 times N minus 2 octets, which corresponds to 120 ms of audio encoded as 10 ms frames in SILK or Hybrid mode at over 1 Mbps. A more reasonable limit is 7,664 times N minus 2 octets, which is 120 ms of audio as 20 ms stereo CELT frames at just under 511 kbps. For family 1, N = 8 gives a size of 61,310 octets, rounded up to a multiple of 1024 octets to give the 61,440 octet packet size that any implementation is expected to handle.

When encoding, a muxer SHOULD take the algorithmic delay of the Opus encoder into account. The number of samples can be queried from encoders derived from the reference implementation. To get good quality in the very first samples, an implementation MAY use linear predictive coding extrapolation to generate at least 120 extra samples at the beginning, so that the encoder is not handed a discontinuous signal. For an input file of a given length, the implementation SHOULD set the pre-skip value to the delay plus the extra samples, encode at least that much plus the length, and set the granule position of the last page to the same total, so that the encoded file has the same duration as the original. The best way to pad the end is also to use extrapolation, though zero-padding is acceptable.

For applications such as Internet radio, it is sometimes useful to cut a long stream into smaller chains so that the comment header can be updated. Encoding each segment independently creates a small discontinuity at the boundary because Opus is lossy. A muxer MAY avoid it by encoding the last frame of the first segment as an independent frame with inter-frame prediction turned off, setting the granule position of the last page near the end of that frame, starting the second segment with a copy of that frame, setting the pre-skip of the second stream so the two join properly, and continuing to encode without resetting the encoder.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets a size limit for audio packets so that a broken file cannot make a player try to allocate gigabytes of memory, and it explains how an encoder should set the timing fields so the played file has the same length as the original.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations of the Opus codec need the security considerations outlined in RFC 4732, and the container is just as much a problem as the codec. Malicious payloads and input streams can be used to attack codec implementations. Implementations MUST NOT overrun their allocated memory nor consume excessive resources when decoding payloads or processing input streams. Problems in encoding are rarer, but the same rule applies to a muxer, because a weakness there would let an attacker attack transcoding gateways.

Header parsing is the most likely place for an overrun. Implementations should make sure their buffers hold enough data for all the required fields before reading them, for example all the channel map data in the identification header, and should validate the channel map indices so that they do not read from channels that do not exist.

To avoid excessive resource use, implementations should be wary of streams that make them process far more data than was actually transmitted. A small comment header can claim string lengths that imply many gigabytes, and even computing the size of the required buffer can overflow a 32-bit integer. After reading the user comment list length, an implementation might check that the header holds at least four octets per comment before going further, taking care to avoid overflow in that calculation too.

A bug seen more than once involves handling invalid data at the end of a stream. Implementations often seek to the end of a stream to find the last timestamp and compute the total duration, and if they do not find a valid capture pattern and page they back up and try again. Without care to avoid rescanning data that was already scanned, that search becomes quadratic in the amount of invalid data. When seeking, implementations should be careful about invalid granule position values and make sure their algorithms keep making progress and eventually terminate, even if values are missing or out of order.

As with most container formats, Ogg Opus streams SHOULD NOT be used with insecure ciphers or cipher modes that are vulnerable to known-plaintext attacks. The page capture pattern and the magic signatures in the two headers have easily predictable values, as do various elements of the codec data itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A broken file can try to make a player allocate far more memory than the file could hold, or send a player round in circles while it searches for the end. The document tells implementations to check lengths before allocating, and to bound their searches.

fields.name: Magic Signature
fields.desc: The ASCII string OpusHead, which identifies the stream as Opus audio.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Always 1 for this specification. The upper four bits are a major version and the lower four a minor version.

fields.name: Channel Count
fields.desc: The number of output channels. It must not be zero and may be as large as 255.

fields.name: Pre-skip
fields.desc: The number of 48 kHz samples to discard at the start of playback, and to subtract from a granule position.

fields.name: Input Sample Rate
fields.desc: The sample rate of the original input in Hz. This is metadata, not the playback rate.

fields.name: Output Gain
fields.desc: A signed Q7.8 fixed-point gain in dB to apply when decoding.

fields.name: Mapping Family
fields.desc: The channel mapping family, followed by the optional channel mapping table.

cells: RTP mapping: mono, or stereo with left and right.
Vorbis channel order, from mono up to 7.1 surround.
A demuxer should behave as though the value were 255.

viz.caption: THE FOUR NUMBERS THAT GIVE A PLAYER THE TIME (RFC 7845, SECTION 4)

items.title: Granule position
items.text: The number of PCM samples in the stream up to the last fully decodable sample on the page, counted at 48 kHz per channel.

items.title: Pre-skip
items.text: The number of samples at the start that are decoder padding rather than real audio, and which the player skips.

items.title: PCM sample position
items.text: The granule position minus the pre-skip. Dividing it by 48000.0 gives the playback time in seconds.

items.title: Pre-roll
items.text: The 80 ms of audio decoded and discarded before a seek target, so that the audio is correct when the target is reached.

fields.name: Magic Signature
fields.desc: The ASCII string OpusTags, which identifies the comment header.

fields.name: Vendor String Length
fields.desc: The length in octets of the vendor string that follows.

fields.name: User Comment List Length
fields.desc: The number of user comments that follow, each with its own 32-bit length and UTF-8 string.
